title: Electromagnetic Induction: How We Make Electricity
hook: Almost all the electricity you use was made by waving magnets past coils of wire. A changing magnetic field pushes charge into motion — that's Faraday's great discovery.
key_points: A changing magnetic field through a coil induces a voltage — Faraday's law of induction.
Faster change or more loops of wire means a bigger induced voltage.
Generators spin coils in a magnetic field; nearly all power plants work this way.
The induced current always opposes the change that made it (Lenz's law), conserving energy.
content_html: In the 1830s Michael Faraday found that a magnet alone does nothing to a nearby wire — but a moving magnet pushes electric charge through it. The rule, Faraday's law of induction, is that a changing magnetic field through a loop of wire creates a voltage across that loop. Move the magnet faster, or add more loops, and the voltage grows. This single fact is how essentially all of our electricity gets made.
extra_html: A generator is just this principle running continuously: spin a coil inside a magnetic field (or spin a magnet past a coil) and you get a steady flow of current. Whatever the energy source — burning coal, splitting atoms, falling water, or wind — a power plant's job is mostly to turn a turbine that turns a generator. There's a catch built into the universe: the induced current always flows in the direction that opposes the change creating it, a rule called Lenz's law. That's not a quirk but a guarantee of energy conservation — otherwise a generator would spin up for free. The same induction underlies transformers, induction stovetops, and the wireless chargers on a desk. Wikipedia traces Faraday's experiments and the law that bears his name.

related.title: Electricity & Magnetism Are One Force
related.hook: Move a magnet near a wire and you make electricity; run current through a wire and you make a magnet. They're two faces of the same force.

related.title: Electric and Magnetic Fields
related.hook: How does a magnet pull a paperclip it isn't touching? Through a field — an invisible region of influence that tells other charges and magnets how to feel a force.

related.title: Electric Charge & Current
related.hook: Everything electrical comes down to charge — and an electric current is simply charge on the move.

flashcards.prompt: What does it take to induce a voltage in a coil of wire?
flashcards.back_html: A changing magnetic field through the coil. A steady field does nothing — it's the change that drives charge into motion (Faraday's law).

flashcards.prompt: How does a typical power plant actually generate electricity?

choices.text: It spins coils of wire in a magnetic field, inducing a current
It chemically creates electric charge from fuel
It stores sunlight and releases it as current at night

flashcards.explanation_html: Coal, gas, nuclear, hydro, and wind plants all spin a turbine that turns a generator — a coil moving in a magnetic field — inducing the current.

flashcards.prompt: Lenz's law says an induced current flows in the direction that…

choices.text: Opposes the change in magnetic field that created it
Reinforces the change, building current without limit
Always flows toward the nearest magnet

flashcards.explanation_html: The induced current opposes the change — if it reinforced it, you'd get energy from nothing. Lenz's law is conservation of energy in action.
